newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma military, student standoff needs resolution.
newsitem.headline: Burma military, student standoff needs resolution.

text.p: Burmese student protests could become more frequent and develop into a major challenge to the military junta unless quick action is taken to address their demands, diplomats said on Sunday.

In the past week the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) has faced its biggest challenge from students since troops crushed student-led pro-democracy uprisings in 1988, leaving thousands dead or in jail.

On Monday and Tuesday, up to 2,000 students from the Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) held street protests demanding more freedom and rights. The protest ended when more than 600 of the original number refused to disperse in central Rangoon and were detained by police on Tuesday before being released.

On Saturday, soldiers and riot police used water cannons and batons to break up a protest by University of Yangon students who refused to disperse despite official pleas. More than 260 students were held briefly and most were later released.
Those students demanded among other things that they be allowed to set up student unions in campuses and the release of 80 colleagues they claimed were detained in a separate incident.

Although the students maintained their protests were non-political, one Western diplomat said they had "more political edges" than previous ones as protest banners also called for freedom, justice, human rights and fair government.
"Basically, the issues remain unresolved. The situation could deteriorate if it became politicised," the diplomat said.
The timing of the protests could not be worse for the SLORC.

International criticism has mounted over its human rights record and failure to recognise a landslide 1990 election victory by the opposition National League for Democracy (NLD) party led by Aung San Suu Kyi
Recent crackdowns on the NLD have also led to calls by Western nations for the delay of Burma's entry into the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
Protesters this week carried pictures of independence hero Aung San, father of Aung San Suu Kyi, reminding people of scenes during the 1988 uprisings.

"Students could easily tack political issues to their demands if they do not get a response from the government...the more protests staged, the more violent they will be. I don't see a quick end to this," one Asian diplomat said.
He said the government, for fear of being embarrassed, had been reluctant to compromise and accept key student demands.
Other diplomats said the SLORC would not allow the organisation of independent student unions on campuses.
Suu Kyi and the NLD have not exploited the student protests and the two sides say they are not linked.
However, political analysts see similarities in their demands for justice and freedom. The students have said they had no links with the Nobel peace laureate.
So far, the SLORC has not said how it plans to deal with the issues raised by the students, although last week official media said students should primarily focus on their studies.
A government spokesman said some access roads to YIT and Yangon University had been blocked on Sunday to keep "political agitators" away from students studying there.

On Saturday, a government official said "soft" measures had been taken so far against the student protesters and the authorities were looking into the problem. However, he gave no details of any measures or solutions planned.

The disturbances have to some extent damaged tourist interest in Burma's "Visit Myanmar Year", which was launched last month in the hope of attracting hundreds of thousands of visitors to the country, diplomats said.

ASEAN, which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam, said on November 30 it would simultaneously admit Burma, Laos and Cambodia as full members of the grouping, but did not say when.
